canberra.title: After losing his veteran father, music helped a Canberra teen heal
canberra.snippet: When Jonathon Nicholas lost his father in October 2024, he wasn’t searching for a stage. He was searching for something to hold on ...
canberra.content:
Jonathon Nicholas performs with his band, Encore. The Year 12 student says music helped him navigate the loss of his veteran father and inspired him to pursue a career in the industry. Photo: Supplied.

When Jonathon Nicholas lost his father in October 2024, he wasn’t searching for a stage. He was searching for something to hold on to.

The Year 12 student at St Edmund’s College had always loved music. It was something he shared with his father, Paul Nicholas, during countless car rides listening to their favourite songs together. But after his father’s death, the guitar became much more than a hobby.

“I didn’t really see any value in going and talking about it,” Jonathon told Region.

“I thought there was probably a better way to channel my feelings.”

At first, music became a distraction. Then it became something much bigger. “It really helped to make sure that I wasn’t spiralling or falling out of control,” he said.

“It really helped to make sure that I stayed on the right path.”

Today, the Canberra teenager is studying Double Music at St Edmund’s College, has formed a band called Encore with friends he has known since kindergarten and is preparing to perform at the Officers’ Spring Ball at Victoria Barracks in Sydney later this year.

Behind the music is the story of a young man finding a way through grief.

Paul Nicholas served in the Australian Army as a Military Police Officer for 27 years and was a Totally and Permanently Incapacitated veteran before his death. Throughout Jonathon’s schooling, the family had received support through the Department of Veterans’ Affairs Education Scheme.

After Paul’s death, the DVA worked with the family to support music tuition as part of Jonathon’s wellbeing plan.

His mother, Kelly Nicholas, said she had recognised her son’s passion for music long before tragedy struck.

She remembers taking him to Better Music in Canberra to try an electric guitar.

“As soon as he sat down and started playing it, I thought, ‘I’m in trouble because that’s going to cost me a lot of money,'” she laughed.

“I could see his passion for it straight away.”

After Paul’s death, that passion became an anchor.

Jonathon immersed himself in music classes at school, where he found comfort in spending time with friends and teachers who understood what he was going through.

“I think one of the first moments I realised it was helping was being able to go to music class, have a laugh with my friends and play music,” he said.

“Before that it was hard to enjoy myself and have fun. Playing music really helped me start feeling a bit better about it.”

Jonathon Nicholas performs with his band, Encore, during a school performance at St Edmund’s College. Photo: Supplied

Kelly said the support her son received extended well beyond the classroom.

His tutor, Den Hanrahan from GTR Tuition, helped build both his confidence and musicianship, while St Edmund’s Head of Clancy House Jeff Vayo and Head of Music Rachel Rasmussen provided constant encouragement as he navigated one of the most difficult periods of his life.

Music has long been part of the Nicholas family’s story. Jonathon’s grandfather, Jon Hayton, was a respected session musician who performed alongside Johnny O’Keefe and The Delltones. During Chuck Berry’s Australian tour in the 1960s, he also performed with the rock-and-roll legend.

Inspired by that musical legacy, and by the music he had shared with his father, Jonathon formed Encore with school friends Ryder Darling, Gordon and Riley, mates he has known since kindergarten.

While the other band members focus on writing and performing, Jonathon has taken on another role.

He manages Encore’s social media, branding and promotion, helping grow the band’s audience beyond Canberra.

“I do all of the social media management and all of the promotion for the band,” he said.

“That’s how we’ve really expanded it and gone from being a little thing in Canberra to now being something bigger.”

There are moments on stage, however, when everything else fades away. “When we’re playing, I like to think that he’s there watching me,” Jonathon said of his father.

“I’ve got all the control, and I’m just kind of watching. I like to think that he’s there watching me, and he knows how I’m feeling.”

He believes his father would have been proud. “I think he’d probably think we’re doing pretty good,” he said.

“And the music is music that he enjoyed, so I think he’d have a good time.”

After finishing Year 12, Jonathon plans to move to Melbourne to study sound engineering, which will allow him to build a career in the music industry while continuing to perform with Encore.

For Kelly, watching her son emerge from unimaginable loss has been its own reward.

“I think the main point is that sometimes through tragedy, you can turn that around,” she said.

“I’m most proud of Jonathon’s resilience.”

To follow Encore, visit Instagram … and they’ll be at Smith’s on 30 August.

canberra.title: Why should we care that H5N1 avian flu is in Australia? Here’s what it means for wildlife, farming and people
canberra.snippet: For the past six years, Australia managed to be free of the highly contagious and deadly H5N1 avian influenza strain. It arrived on Weste...
canberra.content:
At-risk bird species (such as the far eastern curlew) are the priority as Australia grapples with the likely impacts of the deadly H5N1 avian influenza strain that’s reached our shores. Photo: DCCEEW.

For the past six years, Australia managed to be free of the highly contagious and deadly H5N1 avian influenza strain.

It arrived on Western Australia shores on 22 June and has since spread to resident birds in South Australia, Queensland, Victoria and NSW.

The Commonwealth Government has acknowledged that eradication will be impossible and the focus is on trying to keep it out of the agricultural industries for as long as possible and to protect vulnerable native species.

So what is the likelihood that bird species will be wiped out? Can it be passed to livestock and people (which has occurred in the USA)? And what can we expect to see as the virus continues to spread?

Region took part in a briefing with experts from CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness to find out what’s happening behind the announcements and press conferences.

How does this strain compare to others around the world?

Australia has seen some variations of bird flu in the past – such as the H7 outbreak that impacted the poultry industry in 2024.

Viruses constantly mutate, but around 2020/21 the avian flu essentially exchanged gene segments (called reassortments) with local low-pathogenic influenza viruses in North Africa and Europe.

This became the H5N1 plate 2.3.4.4B lineage (similar to how we had different strains of the COVID-19 virus) that has been ravaging the rest of the country for the past six years, decimating not only bird populations but some marine mammal species as well (such as sea lions and elephant seals).

World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) avian influenza expert and CSIRO senior research scientist Dr Frank Wong explained Australia’s strain was known as genotype B3.2 and originally arose from reassortment of the virus in North America.

“[It] then spread to South America in late 2022, moving down the entire west coast of South America in the space of six months, causing great impact to South American poultry industries as well as to wild birdlife and to marine mammals,” he said.

“So that’s why we’re concerned about the introduction of this virus to Australia.”

Dr Wong said “sporadic spillover events” of the virus from birds had occurred in more than 55 mammalian species, categorised into scavenger species, domestic/farm animals and colony mammals.

Wait, so can the virus spread into our livestock and people?

Not at the moment.

The H5N1 strain in Australia has only been detected in resident wild bird species, and hasn’t made its way into poultry or other animals.

But based on what’s happened overseas, it is a possibility.

Dr Wong said the infections in dairy cattle and people in America had been linked to the B3.13 and B1.1 strains of the virus, but reiterated the one in Australia was known as B3.2

“It certainly can infect marine mammals – so, for example, in South America it has impacted colonies of southern elephant seals and sea lions … and when it was detected in Heard Island in late 2025 and early this year, it was observed that it had significant impact to the resident southern elephant seal population … they counted up to 75 per cent of the season’s pup or juvenile population have succumbed to H5N1 infection due to this genotype,” he said.

“The risk with this genotype is still considered low for infection of livestock, and I would add that, aside from just the makeup of the virus or the genotype, you would need an ecological perfect storm for the virus to spill over and impact livestock.”

But given viruses’ predisposition to keep mutating, it’s not out of the question.

“When a virus goes into a new area and it picks up gene segments from local viruses, it could provide a new genotype or a new strain with better host-fitness for host species in that new area,” Dr Wong said.

“[So can transmission to people] occur in Australia? The answer is yes, and that’s why it’s important we keep tracking it.”

CSIRO Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness director Dr Debbie Eagles added this was why a close eye was being kept on every single case to make sure the strain wasn’t changing into something that could cross over.

“If we don’t test, then we’re not able to look for the changes in the sequence that can help to inform if there’s any mutations to the virus that increase the risk of spread to people,” she said.

Is it likely Australian species could go extinct because of this strain?

As the virus has never been in Australia before, we can’t predict exactly how it will interact with the biology of our native species.

But it’s already well documented to have devastating impacts on poultry populations, and a mass extinction event of greater crested terns at Baudin Rocks, south of Cape Jaffa in South Australia, has already been reported.

Dr Wong said the level of an extinction event in Australia would come down to the species that had been infected.

“In species that are pretty healthy in terms of their population status, and have a lot of big numbers, there’s been reports that, over subsequent seasons, that population … has had signs of recovery,” he explained.

“But in populations where there’s already critical [low] numbers and are already hammered by other conservation impacts … then you could risk an extinction-level impact because those particular species would find it much more challenging to recover from … highly pathogenic bird flu on top of that.”

What about vaccines? What’s going to be protected?

Vulnerable bird species that are in captivity are being prioritised to receive two shots of a bird flu vaccine.

These are sourced from overseas and Australia doesn’t have the capability to produce them here at the moment.

And it’s unclear if poultry farms will be given access to the vaccine either.

“There’s ongoing discussion between government and industry about whether that might be feasible, sort of what opportunities and risks there might be around that,” Dr Eagles said.

“Obviously there’s a number of measures that can be implemented as needed, such as the Victorian housing orders that have been put in place … all of those additional biosecurity measures can help where they’re specifically needed.”

Anyone who encounters sick or dead wildlife should avoid touching the animal, record it with a phone and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. More information can be found at Agriculture.

canberra.title: Greek comfort food meets family-style hospitality at Asteri Greek Taverna
canberra.snippet: Swinger Hill is now home to a Greek restaurant that is as delicious as it is gregarious. Asteri Greek Taverna is named after the village ...
canberra.content:
The grilled octopus was fabulous with a glass of retsina. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Swinger Hill is now home to a Greek restaurant that is as delicious as it is gregarious. Asteri Greek Taverna is named after the village where owner and chef Tim ‘Digger’ Moustakas’s mother was born. There’s a family-style ease here, and a sense of comfort.

Chef Digger previously ran Fillos at Hellenic Club Woden before moving to Swinger Hill to open Asteri earlier this year.

Having arrived on a bitterly cold and rainy night, we’re eager to shake off the chill. We quickly decide on the grilled octopus as my dining partner reminisces about the meals she ate on a Greek holiday. We also order moussaka – a classic – and keftedes, which are described as Greek meatballs.

I am intrigued by a dish under the salads heading called horta: boiled endive with olive oil and lemon juice, served with home-made bread. Our server suggests we have that with the octopus to start.

There is also a ‘Digger-station’ menu option for those wanting a broader taste of the menu (and a dose of Chef Digger’s humour!)

The olive oil really elevated this dish of wilted greens with lemon. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

My friend enthusiastically orders us two glasses of retsina: a Greek white wine with a unique pine flavour. It’s a ‘love it’ or ‘hate it’ kind of drink. Some find the flavour a little too reminiscent of Pine-O-Clean, or too strong, but we fall into the ‘love it’ category!

The octopus arrives quickly, and we tuck in. This dish is available as an entree or main dish, and the entree comes with two well-sized tentacles on a bed of bean puree. The meat is tender, perfectly charred and spiced with just a hint of cinnamon. The horta endive does make a nice accompaniment to the dish. The greens are sweet and tasty, and although it’s a simple dish, the quality of the olive oil makes the whole thing shine. Big yum.

Moussaka is a well-loved Greek dish made with layers of eggplant, potato and minced meat, topped with cheese. The Asteri version also has a layer of rice on the bottom, which is mixed with greens.

We are immediately enamoured by this herby delight and very pleased when we see that the keftedes meatballs are served on top of a pile of the stuff!

It’s a hearty, warming dish and exactly what we need on this cold night. The keftedes are gorgeous: tender, juicy and packed with flavour. They are a delight with plenty of lemon squeezed on top.

Mousaka is a classic Greek dish, and this version is excellent. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Both dishes come with a side of moreish lemon-baked potatoes and a Greek salad. I love Greek salad, but fresh tomatoes, cucumbers and capsicum are far from their best in a Canberra winter. This creates something of a conundrum: can a Greek restaurant not serve Greek salad? It’s not for me to decide, but next time I’d personally swap it for the more seasonal cabbage salad until we get to summer.

At this point we’re ready for another glass of wine. My friend is ready for more retsina, but I’m curious about the other Greek wines on the menu. I’m not particularly well-versed in Greek wine varieties, so I ask for a recommendation. Our server gives me a taste of vidiano from Heraklion in Crete. It’s a dry white with stone-fruit aromatics and a savoury finish. I get a glass and enjoy it very much.

The kefetedes were a new dish to us but a quick favourite. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

We sticky-beak on the orders of surrounding tables. One group has ordered different types of souvlaki that look really good; the chicken skewers, in particular, are giving me order-envy. I’d come back for that, or to try the Greek-style pizzas which look like a good time.

We are full but determined to taste at least one dessert and find ourselves drawn to rice pudding, described on the menu as Yiayia’s delight. Topped with cinnamon and served with caramelised fig ice-cream, the dish is creamy and comforting. We mop up every bite.

Swinger Hill is lucky to have Asteri as their local!

Asteri Greek Taverna is located at Swinger Hill Shops, 84 Ainsworth St, Mawson. They are open for lunch from 12 pm to 2:30 pm, seven days a week and for dinner from 6 pm to 9 pm Monday to Wednesday and from 6 pm to 10 pm Thursday to Sunday. Follow Asteri on Facebook or Instagram.

canberra.title: Broulee Ocean Swimmers reckon they have the recipe to longevity
canberra.snippet: Most mornings a very happy group of people meet in Broulee to swim laps together in Shark Bay. They are not training for anything. What b...
canberra.content:
Members of the Broulee Ocean Swimmers group in Fiji. Photos: Supplied.

Most mornings a very happy group of people meet in Broulee to swim laps together in Shark Bay.

They are not training for anything. What brings them together is a love of the ocean, wanting to keep fit and enjoying the company of like-minded people.

Earlier this month, nine of them swapped Broulee’s currently chilly waters for a swim trek in the crystal-clear waters of Fiji. Ranging in age from 57 to 87, they swam between one and three kilometres each day amid eye-catching fish and vibrant coral reefs.

Gillian Stapleton has been a member of the Broulee Ocean Swimmers for just over a year. She said it was a community swim, along the lines of a community run.

In the warmer months, upwards of 20 local swimmers, plus visitors, congregate at 8:30 am to swim in Shark Bay. Right now, only a few are pulling on wetsuits, caps, booties and gloves each day to brave the elements.

Ms Stapleton said the swimmers came from all walks of life and were generally aged from 35 years. Their oldest member, who is 87, swam every day in Fiji.

“Wendy is in the ocean most days and is just so engaged with life,” Ms Stapleton said. “She inspires me to do it.”

Nine members of the Broulee Ocean Swimmers went on a swim trek to Fiji.

An accomplished marathon runner, Ms Stapleton is relatively new to swimming. She took stroke correction classes and is now addicted to ocean swimming.

“We swam one or three kilometres a day in Fiji,” she said. “A year ago, I never thought I would be swimming those distances.”

Others in the group have lived in Broulee for years and are very seasoned swimmers.

The Broulee Ocean Swimmers generally swim one or two kilometres each day, but Ms Stapleton was not doing anything near that when she first joined. It is possible to do as little as 200 metres.

“They are such an inclusive group and people give you tips and hints,” she said. “You come back because you think to yourself you can do this.”

One of the members heard about the tour company that runs Ocean Swim Fiji. Nine of them used the swim trek to set goals and train for the week-long event.

“Swim treks are a big thing,” Ms Stapleton said. “You go there for a week, and you swim every day and get to swim in gorgeous places.”

There were about 55 swimmers at the Fiji event. Anyone can join, but Ms Stapleton said that the Fiji one sold out within an hour.

Members of the Broulee Ocean Swimmers group.

The Broulee Ocean Swimmers grew from a group of swimmers who meet at 9 am every Sunday at South Broulee in the summer for a 1.4-kilometre swim.

While not an officially sanctioned Surf Life Saving event, the swim is held within sight of the Broulee Surfers Surf Life Saving Club who have a patrol on duty most Sundays during summer.

Ms Stapleton said ocean swimming and swimming treks were growing in popularity because of the sense of belonging and wellbeing they promoted, and the good conversations that swimmers had. It was about far more than laps.

“It’s a tight-knit community that shows up for each other, cheers each other on, and makes growing older feel like something to look forward to rather than something to fight,” she said.

“That sense of belonging, by their own account, is a big part of what’s kept them so active well into their 70s and 80s. It is proof that connection and consistency go hand in hand with longevity.”

Original Article published by Marion Williams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Canberra’s about to lose so much more than access to library books
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s public libraries will shortly become less accessible. The public weren’t consulted, the changes have been poorly explained, an...
canberra.content:
David Still is campaigning for better public library opening hours in the ACT. Photo: Supplied.

Canberra’s public libraries will shortly become less accessible. The public weren’t consulted, the changes have been poorly explained, and the transition won’t be seamless.

Canberrans have made it clear that they don’t want this.

Here’s why.

What’s changing?

First, the good news. If you use Kingston library, you’re gaining four hours per week – the only library that will see an improvement. If you need to go to the library at 9 am, you soon can.

Saturday hours will be slightly increased at five branches. And … that’s it.

By contrast, losses are significant. Every library will now close on Sundays. Three branches will also close on Saturdays, and we’re losing late evening hours at Woden, Gungahlin and Dickson.

If you work office hours, you’ll possibly never see Civic, Erindale or Kippax Libraries open again.

These changes fall short of national standards, despite the ACT Government’s claims.

It pretends Canberra is one catchment area – probably news to residents of Calwell, who are 35 km away from Gungahlin Library.

The reality is that people don’t travel across town to visit libraries.

It would have been more honest to consider each library’s community.

In this respect, we fail.

Belconnen, with a population of 106,061, will have a library with only 48 hours of opening time per week, 16 hours less than the standard. Tuggeranong, home to 89,461 people, falls short by 8 hours per week.

Why is this happening?

The changes spring from a 2025 private member’s motion by Andrew Braddock, which called for investment in ACT public libraries.

This led to the Libraries ACT Independent Working Group Report (‘the LACT report’). The report was a disaster.

The executive summary is a shopping list of organisational issues: “a complex and deeply embedded set of cultural, operational, and systemic issues that have significantly impacted staff morale, engagement, organisational cohesion and decreased community service delivery.”

The report did review opening hours. Most worryingly, staff working evenings at Dickson were worried about occupational violence. As a paramedic, this is unacceptable. If those staff will now feel safe, I support them.

As for the rest, the recommendations were mild and reasonable. It recommended a review of hours, changes to the Christmas period, and a reduction in late-night hours at Dickson. It didn’t recommend reduced hours anywhere else.

In fact, it recommended increased staffing, and an additional $1.7 million in funding – the government equivalent of digging for loose change down the back of the couch.

We found $7.155 million in direct funding to the horse-racing industry through Thoroughbred Park, but we can’t find a quarter of that for our libraries?

The visitation data doesn’t support cuts either. Amazingly, Civic, Kingston and Kippax all have their highest patronage per hour on Saturdays, but two of these will now close on those days.

Even the libraries with ‘quiet’ weekends are only a little slower on Saturday and Sunday. The fact is that people love weekend library hours.

What will we lose?

The answer depends on who you are, and it goes well beyond losing a place where you can borrow Project Hail Mary for a family night in. (Although, you should still do that.)

If you’re a working parent in the West Belconnen area, you’ll lose the most. The Saturday ‘Giggle and Wiggle’ program is a hugely successful event for kids, which regularly gets 90-plus attendees.

It’s a critical support for new parents, but it will run for the last time on 22 August. The promised replacement at Belconnen hasn’t been confirmed yet.

Public transport users will also lose out. A Ginninderry family will now take three times longer to reach their nearest library on a Saturday bus.

Proximity is accessibility, and as new suburbs like Macnamara continue to fill the western borders of Canberra, more parents will find themselves without access to libraries.

In total, parts of 26 suburbs will be at least 45 minutes by Saturday public transport from their closest libraries. If you can’t afford to live centrally, public libraries aren’t for you.

Book-borrowers, you lose too. The minister has promised ‘parcel locker’-style collection boxes – cheaper than staff, I guess – but they will open this month.

They’re promised for “late 2026”.

Finally, we’re losing a free ‘third space’ during a cost-of-living crisis. The minister has been careful to say that community rooms will still be available for bookings, but speaking from recent experience, it is not easy to book a room you’ve never seen with your own eyes.

There’s one more thing we’ll lose: a way back. The minister reassured us that visitation data will be reviewed, but this is survivorship bias – a classic problem with bad statistics.

If you’re designing bombers in World War II, this might lead you to armour all the least critical parts of the aircraft because you only studied the ones that came back covered in holes – you missed the ones that never came home.

If you’re designing library opening hours, you’ll only study people who attended during opening hours. You’ll never know that the public demands longer hours – you stopped looking at 5 pm.

The minister’s reassurance is empty.

So what can we do about this?

Sign the petition, along with 2700 of my closest friends. If you already have, you can email Minister Tara Cheyne directly: cheyne@act.gov.au

After all, Ginninderra – her electorate – will be worst off.

David Still is the chief petitioner calling for increased investment in public libraries to keep them open on weekends.

australia.title: First Australian death of little penguin with H5 bird flu confirmed on Phillip Island
australia.snippet: Authorities confirm first Australian death of species found with virus near where it attracts crowds to a ‘penguin parade’ Get our breaki...
australia.content:
Australia’s first case of the deadly H5 bird flu in a little penguin has been confirmed on Victoria’s Phillip Island, only days after the state government announced it would begin vaccinating the species.

Confirmation of the virus in the little penguin will spark a race to vaccinate thousands of birds, with the government announcing on Saturday it would begin the rollout on Monday.

The government did not provide the exact location where the bird was found, but said it was not inside the island’s famous penguin parade area.

A spokesperson confirmed the little penguin had died.

There are about 40,000 little penguins on Phillip Island, making it the world’s biggest colony of the species and a major tourist attraction.

Environment advocates have been concerned about the potential for mass deaths of little penguins if the virus reached the island.

Euan Ritchie, a professor in wildlife ecology and conservation at Deakin university, said the detection of H5 bird flu in the much-loved little penguin population was “devastating”.

“Phillip Island is home to a diverse array and significant populations of native wildlife, including Australian fur seals, eastern barred bandicoots, and recently reintroduced bush stone curlews,” he said.

“Governments must provide whatever resources are needed to help wildlife survive through and recover from this bird flu outbreak.”

On Wednesday, the Victorian government announced plans for the world’s largest H5 bird flu vaccination program of wild birds.

The government said it would vaccinate up to 5,000 little penguins across populations at Phillip Island and at Melbourne’s St Kilda beach. While vaccinating wild birds is challenging, it was considered possible in Victoria’s wild little penguins because they generally return to the same burrows at Phillip Island and St Kilda each night.

But vaccination requires the delivery of two doses with a gap of a few weeks between each dose.

The detection on Phillip Island will spark concern that it may be too late for some little penguins to develop immunity.

Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said he understood Victorians would be worried about the detection of the deadly virus in a little penguin.

“We know that the detection in a little penguin on Phillip Island is of concern,” he said.

“But we are proceeding with vaccination of the little penguin colony on Phillip Island and at St Kilda as a meaningful way in which it can help mitigate the impact of H5 on those populations.

“We know that little penguins are iconic and highly valued by Victorians, and for that reason, we are working as a priority to protect those colonies.”

The state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said Agriculture Victoria and Phillip Island Nature Parks “activated plans” to vaccinate little penguins as soon as the federal government authorised the vaccines for priority native bird species.

“Agriculture Victoria is working closely with Phillip Island Nature Parks to support vaccination of little penguins from Monday,” he said.

“While the first detection in a little penguin is a concern, vaccination of little penguins on Phillip Island remains a meaningful way to help protect this important colony.”

The Victorian government said there had been two further detections of H5 in greater crested terns, one at Lakes Entrance and the other at Dromana on the Mornington peninsula.

Todd said the Lakes Entrance detection was significant because it showed the virus was continuing to move through wild bird populations across Victoria.

On Saturday, the NSW government also confirmed the fifth detected case in the state, in a tern found at Eden on the far south coast.

The government said it would increase surveillance in the area as a result.

There have been two other confirmed cases in local birds in the state, one at Narooma on the state’s south coast and one at Wentworth in the far south-west. All of the confirmed cases in local birds have been in greater crested terns.

australia.title: ‘My heart breaks into a million pieces’: emotional tributes to Kumanjayi Little Baby at Alice Springs funeral
australia.snippet: Hundreds gathered with flashes of pink to farewell the five-year-old girl, who was allegedly murdered in April Warning: This story contai...
australia.content:
A sombre funeral service for Kumanjayi Little Baby has been attended by hundreds of people from the Alice Springs community and surrounds.

Wearing pink and some dressed in T-shirts bearing the face of the five-year-old girl, the crowd gathered under grey skies in the red centre capital on Saturday.

Family members surrounded a small coffin adorned with flowers and cried together.

The girl’s grandfather, Robin Japanangka Granites, opened the funeral to the public to allow the community to grieve as one.

“You come because you are one of our family,” he told them.

“You are from here and we need you because we both cried at that same time.”

In a eulogy read on her behalf, Kumanjayi Little Baby’s mother, Jacinta Roy, urged that her daughter be remembered for who she was.

She was a girl who loved watching shows like Masha and the Bear and Bluey, as well as playing games on her mum’s phone, Roy said.

The young girl also loved cuddling puppies and the colour pink.

“As a mother, my heart breaks into a million pieces,” she said. “I miss her.

“As a Christian, I would like to thank Father, Son and Holy Spirit for gifting me with a beautiful, precious little baby girl for the precious time that I was her mother here on Earth.”

The family of the allegedly murdered girl invited the desert community to farewell her on Saturday while embracing her favourite colour, pink.

The service comes months after her disappearance sparked one of the largest searches in Northern Territory history.

Kumanjayi Little Baby – as she is known for cultural reasons after her death – went missing on the outskirts of Alice Springs in late April.

It prompted an intensive five-day search by emergency services and local volunteers in grassy bushland.

The discovery of her body prompted a nationwide outpouring of grief, with vigils held across the country.

A 47-year-old man is awaiting trial after being charged with her murder.

Japanangka Granites, a Warlpiri elder, thanked locals for their efforts to locate Kumanjayi Little Baby and for their support of his family.

Kumanjayi Little Baby would be with our “father in heaven”, he said at the time.

  • Indigenous Australians can call 13YARN on 13 92 76 for information and crisis support; or call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Mensline on 1300 789 978

australia.title: Coalition split on Andrew Bragg speech as South Australian senator Andrew McLachlan urges colleagues to ‘follow his lead’
australia.snippet: Senior colleagues dismiss Bragg’s migration figures as ‘personal views’ while others say critical response is an ‘overreaction’ Get our b...
australia.content:
The Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has publicly backed Andrew Bragg and urged colleagues to “follow his lead” after a public speech that has split colleagues and triggered a rebuke from the opposition leader, Angus Taylor.

At the National Press Club on Wednesday, Bragg announced a policy to slash the national construction code and suggested net overseas migration should be dropped from the current level of about 300,000 to below 180,000 a year to keep pace with new housing builds.

Senior colleagues, including Taylor, were quick to dismiss the migration figure this week, saying they were Bragg’s “personal views” and that the party’s policy was yet to be finalised. The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said: “I don’t think you should bank that at all” in response to the number.

Privately, Taylor counselled his frontbencher.

Moderates, including McLachlan and the Queensland senator Paul Scarr, called Bragg’s speech “terrific” while others privately said the reaction by the media and some internally was “overblown”.

McLachlan, an outspoken South Australian senator who has publicly criticised his party’s positions on migration and the climate crisis, said Bragg “delivered a masterclass in thought leadership”.

“His address was an important step in the development of a policy suite that seeks to advance the nation,” McLachlan told Guardian Australia.

“His aspiration for Australia is admirable. Every member of the Coalition should follow his lead and discuss policy pathways openly.”

Scarr, who has also defied his party and crossed the Senate floor in March to censure Pauline Hanson after she wore a burqa in the upper house, said he “thought it was a terrific speech. High-level and reinforcing our core Liberal values”.

Other Liberals have been frustrated at the intervention by Bragg, with one MP saying privately colleagues were angry at the lack of discipline and this could be “his last chance”.

Even after critical commentary from his colleagues in recent days, Bragg has maintained it was important to talk about big ideas.

The NSW senator said while many of his ideas, such as a specific net overseas migration target, hadn’t been greenlit by the shadow cabinet, it was important to “move the debate on”.

Bragg said voters needed “ambitious policy for tomorrow, not micro-announcements for today that aim to please and appease”.

“I’m confident that we will be rewarded for putting more detail on the table,” he told Guardian Australia.

On Friday, the shadow housing minister also corrected comments made in an interview on RN Breakfast where he responded “yes, definitely”, when asked whether Australians should accept substandard homes under his changes to the construction code, which would make energy efficiency standards voluntary.

In a social media post, Bragg said he had misheard the question, adding “houses built to this standard would be strong, safe and sound homes with all the basic amenity, such as insulation, plumbing, sewerage etc”.

“I did not intend to agree that houses complying with the Basic Australian Standard would be ‘substandard’. They wouldn’t be.”

One Liberal MP, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said there had been overreaction to the speech internally, which likely came from “not reading what was actually in the speech”.

“Like any disruption, you might be a bit uncomfortable first. I think maybe just a little bit of surprise for some. I think he did a good job and he was brave.”

They welcomed the fresh take from Bragg and said the Sydney senator consistently showed he wasn’t a “benchwarmer”, but wanted to engage in substantial policy.

“Clearly what we’ve been doing over the last five or six years in particular has not worked. So maybe taking a different approach or approaching the problem in a different way is a sensible thing to do.”

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, was quick to shoot down any cuts to working holiday visas as Bragg suggested in his speech, but praised his “big ideas”.

“I love Andrew Bragg. He’s he’s full of ideas … we need people like him because he’s full of energy and enthusiasm,” he told ABC’s Radio National on Friday.

australia.title: Fears for missing Sydney teen who hasn’t been seen since leaving for hike on Wednesday
australia.snippet: Fresh search teams to scour Nattai national park for Lily Hooper, 18, who failed to return home from a bushwalk Get our breaking news ema...
australia.content:
The search for an 18-year-old bushwalker missing in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales since Wednesday is continuing, with fresh teams arriving at the Nattai national park on Saturday morning.

Lily Hooper left her home in Sydney’s south-west about 8am on 12 August, after telling family she was going for a hike in the national park, north-west of Mittagong.

The experienced hiker was reported missing when she did not return that evening and could not be reached, despite having sent messages from the park earlier in the day.

A search began with her car found parked on Wanganderry Road, near the start of the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail at High Range, about 11pm that night.

On Saturday, NSW police said in a statement that initial inquiries indicated Hooper reached the summit of Bonnum Pic about mid-morning on Wednesday, but had made no further contact since then.

A multi-agency search – involving local police, regional Police Rescue, NSW Ambulance, Fire and Rescue NSW, the State Emergency Service and members of Hooper’s family – has not found any further signs of the teen.

Defence force personnel joined the search on Friday, with drones, an ambulance helicopter and specialist rescuers, including trail-bike riders, also involved.

A NSW police spokesperson said the search continued overnight and fresh teams arrived at the park at 7am on Saturday.

On Friday, Det Insp Benjamin Bowles said authorities were concerned for Hooper’s safety.

But he said he remained optimistic, and that Hooper was an experienced hiker.

“We have not been able to fully confirm what supplies [Hooper] had with her at the time, but we are still hopeful that we will be able to locate her safe and sound,” he said.

“We don’t have any information to suggest that this is anything other than an overdue hiker.”

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, told reporters on Friday he was “praying for good news”.

“Our heart goes out to that young walker’s family,” he said. “We know this must be heartbreaking and incredibly anxious.”

Hooper is described as Caucasian in appearance, about 175cm tall, slim, and with long blond hair and blue eyes. She was last seen wearing a shirt and shorts, but police said it was not known what clothing or supplies she took for the hike.

Police said anyone who may have seen Hooper, had information about her whereabouts or who walked the Bonnum Pic walking trail on Wednesday, should contact Moss Vale police station on 02 4869 7899 or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

world.title: American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months
world.snippet: Kevin Rideout, who was abducted by unknown assailants in Niamey, said to be in good health and in care of US officials An American missio...
world.content:
An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said.

Serving in Mission International said Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family.

Donald Trump, who claimed to have helped secure Rideout’s release, later said he was “back in United States Custody” on Friday.

The 50-year-old missionary pilot was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Other details about his rescue remain unknown.

The US president’s administration had made the release of Rideout a priority in its latest strategy on African Sahel states, after years of fighting extremism found limited success. Rideout had been working in Niger for 19 years as a missionary before the incident.

“I am proud to announce that Kevin Rideout, a wonderful Christian Missionary, is back in United States Custody,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Friday. “Kevin, the United States of America looks forward to welcoming you HOME. Glad to have helped!”

Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State. A “continually deteriorating security situation” across the country was cited by the military junta that took power in 2023 when deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum.

The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia. One former US base has since been occupied by Russian soldiers.

Trump described the broader region of west Africa as “the epicenter of Islamist terrorism” in his social media post on Friday, claiming there had been “more deadly attacks in the past year” there than anywhere else on Earth.

Washington has since shifted its focus to coastal west African states including Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana, sharing intelligence with local security personnel to prevent extremist threats from spilling southwards from the arid Sahel.

However, the insurgency continues to escalate in the region. In Niger, data from Acled, the armed conflict data aggregator, shows that civilian fatalities rose by nearly 50% in the year after Bazoum was ousted.

Cities and urban centres in the Sahel region have also been increasingly targeted by armed non-state actors as the crisis reaches new dimensions.

The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”.

In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport, a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the Alliance of Sahel States, the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

In April, Mali’s defence minister, Gen Sadio Camara, was killed in his home on the outskirts of the capital Bamako during coordinated assaults staged by insurgents including the west African affiliate of al-Qaida.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

world.title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province
world.snippet: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever The Ebola outbreak in th...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.

The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.

Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.

The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.

The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.

Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.

The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.

Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.

Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”

Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.

Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.

This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.

Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.

world.title: French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women
world.snippet: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence France has opened disciplina...
world.content:
France has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador to Central African Republic over allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.

The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.

The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.

The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.

The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”

The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.

Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.

According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.

He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.

Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.

French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” between France and CAR when he visited Bangui in March.

world.title: Zambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rival
world.snippet: Hakainde Hichilema is bidding for second term, but feud between him and family of Edgar Lungu, who died in 2025, continues As Zambians go...
world.content:
As Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections.

Hakainde Hichilema, 64, is bidding for a second term leading the southern African country after defeating his arch-rival Edgar Lungu by a landslide in 2021.

A feud between the two men, their families and supporters has dominated Zambian politics, to the extent that the quarrel has continued even after Lungu died in South Africa in June 2025.

Zambia’s government went to court to try to stop the burial of Lungu by his family, who did not want Hichilema presiding over a state funeral. In June, South Africa’s supreme court of appeal ruled in favour of Lungu’s family, overturning a previous high court decision in favour of the government.

In this election, Hichilema is facing the Tonse Alliance of opposition parties led by Brian Mundubile, 55, who was a government chief whip under Lungu. Mundubile’s running mate Makebi Zulu acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson during the burial row, and on the campaign trail the two men have promised to bring Lungu’s body back to Zambia for a dignified burial.

The way death is dealt with is very important in Zambia, said Christopher Vandome, a senior research fellow at the thinktank Chatham House. “Even Hichilema supporters want to see due respect given to those that have died,” he said. “When it appears things get messy, it just makes the incumbent look disrespectful.”

The shadow of Lungu has also hung over allegations by the Tonse Alliance that Hichilema has deployed authoritarian tactics during the election campaign, including raiding its offices and detaining 36 members of Mundubile’s team.

Hichilema’s team furiously denied the claims, invoking Lungu’s treatment of Hichilema during the last election. “Zambians know what repression looks like. In 2021, the opposition leader [Hichilema] had been arrested 15 times, Prime TV [a private station] and the Post [a newspaper] had been shut down, and on election day the internet was switched off,” said a spokesperson for the ruling United Party for National Development. “Today the opposition campaigns freely across all 10 provinces, no media house has been closed and the airwaves are open.”

Transparency International Zambia monitors have recorded incidents of police interrupting opposition rallies, said Tamika Halwiindi, a coordinator at the organisation. “Disruptions from the police citing issues to do with safety have been noted to be more biased against the opposition and independents, as opposed to … the ruling party,” she said.

During Hichilema’s term, activists have also reported having peaceful demonstrations shut down. Mputa Ngalande of the Fight Inequality Alliance said he was among a group detained for more than 12 hours in July 2024 when they were protesting against the state power company during a period of 22-hour-a-day blackouts.

Vandome said: “[Hichilema’s] prospects of winning are very high. But his … personal lived experience of how complicated Zambian elections can be has given him this insecurity which is actually counting against him … denting his image in a way he doesn’t have to.”

Zambia’s economy has stabilised since an economic crisis, which was triggered when it defaulted on its debts in 2020 under Lungu. Annual inflation is now 6.5%, compared with 24.6% in July 2021. The government made primary and secondary education free in 2022.

Meanwhile, Zambia has attracted more international investment in recent years due to its huge deposits of copper, a key material in green technologies.

At the start of the month, in a giveaway to young voters, Hichilema, also known by his initials HH and nickname Bally (a slang word for an elder), told a crowd of jubilant university students that he was increasing their accommodation allowance by 50% with immediate effect.

However, the cost of living could still count against Hichilema in the elections, in which almost 8.8 million registered voters will also choose MPs and local councillors. The average annual income rose from $1,127 to $1,318 between 2021 and 2025, according to World Bank data. But prices almost doubled over the same period.

“What people are asking is: ‘If we are doing well economically, why are we not feeling impact on the ground?’” said Ngalende. “Because you will find on the ground that it is very difficult to access three meals a day.”

world.title: At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe
world.snippet: Operation under way to rescue dozens missing after boat overturned by waves at world’s largest human-made lake At least 44 people have di...
world.content:
At least 44 people have died after an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, police said.

The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales.

A crew member told the national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passenger told ZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps.

A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing.

Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon in posts on X twice in the space of 32 minutes. In the first post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.

A video shared by ZBC on Tuesday showed several people appearing to be sitting on the upturned ferry, while at least four speedboats came to their aid and a helicopter circled overhead.

Maxwell Kanhema Page, who describes himself as a media practitioner and originally posted the video shared by ZBC, reshared a video on his Facebook page filmed from the shore, in which he had noted that the lake was “angry”.

He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity.

It is not uncommon for boats to overturn on the lake. In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five drowned in a 2021 incident and three were feared dead in an October 2023 capsizing. The month before, a police boat overturned although no one died.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report.
